Once in the brain, it interferes with neuronal protein synthesis, which can lead to mercury poisoning1. This manifests clinically as severe neurological damage, ataxia (loss of coordination), tremors, and behavioral changes.

description:
While many cats love the taste of tuna, it should not be a regular part of their diet. A tiny flake of plain, cooked tuna packed in water is generally safe as a rare treat, but a diet that includes a lot of tuna can lead to serious health problems.

Feeding cats raw tuna is especially risky because it contains an enzyme called thiaminase, which destroys thiamine (Vitamin B1), a nutrient essential for a healthy nervous system. A diet heavy in any kind of tuna can also lead to mercury poisoning over time, causing neurological damage. Furthermore, tuna is high in certain fats but lacks Vitamin E, an imbalance that can cause a painful inflammatory condition called steatitis, or "yellow fat disease."

To be safe, never feed your cat raw tuna. Avoid tuna packed in oil or brine, as the high fat and salt content are unhealthy. Tuna should only be an occasional treat, not a meal. If your cat has been eating a tuna-heavy diet, it is best to consult with a veterinarian.
emergencyNote: Because tuna toxicity in cats is generally the result of chronic, long-term feeding
name: Tuna
safetyNotes: Thiaminase risk: raw tuna contains thiaminase, which destroys thiamine (B1); regular raw tuna feeding causes neurological damage — weakness, head tilt, seizures
Mercury risk: tuna is high in mercury; chronic exposure causes neurological damage, kidney damage, and immune suppression
Nutritional imbalance: tuna alone lacks several essential nutrients for cats (calcium, vitamins) and is high in unsaturated fats that deplete vitamin E
Canned tuna in water (plain, no salt): safe as an occasional treat; avoid tuna in oil or with any added salt
A small piece of plain cooked tuna occasionally is fine; daily feeding is not recommended

Steatitis (Yellow Fat Disease)
symptoms.notes: Tuna is extremely high in polyunsaturated fatty acids but naturally lacks adequate Vitamin E2. A heavy tuna diet depletes the cat's Vitamin E reserves, causing the fat tissue to oxidize and become painfully inflamed.
symptoms.onset: Chronic (develops over weeks to months of a diet heavy in tuna).

symptoms.name: Neurological Dysfunction (Methylmercury Poisoning)
symptoms.notes: Because tuna is a large apex predator, it bioaccumulates high levels of methylmercury2. Cats are particularly sensitive to low doses of organic mercury, which easily crosses the blood-brain barrier and interferes with neuronal protein synthesis.
symptoms.onset: Chronic (accumulates over time with regular feeding).

symptoms.name: Neurological Dysfunction (Thiamine Deficiency) (Note
symptoms.notes: Raw tuna (such as Skipjack and Yellowfin) can contain thiaminase, an enzyme that destroys thiamine (Vitamin B1)6. Lack of thiamine halts cellular energy metabolism and causes a potentially fatal "Wernicke-like" encephalopathy.
symptoms.onset: Chronic / Delayed (typically develops within 2 to 4 weeks of a raw fish-heavy diet).

symptoms.name: Gastrointestinal Upset and Salt Toxicosis (Note
symptoms.notes: Human-grade canned tuna is frequently packed in oil or high-sodium brine12. The high fat content in oil-packed tuna can trigger severe digestive upset or acute pancreatitis910.
symptoms.onset: Acute (within hours to a few days of ingestion).

treatments.name: Because tuna toxicity in cats is generally the result of chronic, long-term feeding

treatments.description: of the procedure: A veterinarian administers targeted pain-relieving medications to manage the cat's discomfort. In severe cases, surgical intervention may be required to physically remove the inflamed, affected fatty tissue.
treatments.name: Pain Management and Surgical Excision (For Steatitis)
treatments.notes: This is an urgent priority if the cat has developed steatitis (also known as "yellow fat disease"). A diet heavy in tuna lacks adequate Vitamin E and is too high in polyunsaturated fats, which triggers this exquisitely painful inflammation of the cat's fat tissue.

treatments.description: of the procedure: The veterinarian administers high doses of thiamine (typically 100–300 mg/day via intravenous or intramuscular injection initially, followed by oral supplements) until the cat's clinical signs resolve.
treatments.name: Thiamine (Vitamin B1) Supplementation (For Raw Tuna)
treatments.notes: This is a critical, life-saving intervention if the cat has been eating raw tuna. Raw fish contains thiaminase, an anti-nutritional enzyme that destroys Vitamin B145.

treatments.description: of the procedure: Immediately discontinuing the feeding of tuna and transitioning the cat to a nutritionally complete, balanced feline diet recommended by a veterinarian.
treatments.name: Dietary Modification and Nutritional Correction
treatments.notes: This is the most essential foundational treatment for all tuna-induced health issues. Human-grade tuna lacks essential feline nutrients such as taurine and Vitamin E, and feeding it regularly exposes the cat to dangerous accumulations of heavy metals like methylmercury28. Removing tuna from the diet.

treatments.description: of the procedure: Providing general supportive treatments to resolve digestive upset, which may include anti-nausea medications (antiemetics) and potentially intravenous fluids to correct dehydration.
treatments.name: Symptomatic Gastrointestinal Support
treatments.notes: Tuna intended for human consumption can cause acute digestive upset in cats1. This treatment is applied if the cat develops vomiting or diarrhea after eating human-grade canned tuna, particularly if it was packed in oil or a high-sodium brine.
